subject: Cognitive Science
title: Ambiguity Aversion
description: A quick win: understand Ambiguity Aversion.

hook.text: Urn A has 50 red and 50 black balls. Urn B has 100 balls, unknown mix. Most people choose Urn A. Why?

buildup.text: Daniel Ellsberg showed that people prefer known probabilities over unknown ones—even when the math is identical.

discovery.text: This is ambiguity aversion: uncertainty about the odds feels worse than the odds themselves.

twist.text: In real life, most risks involve ambiguity, not clean probabilities. We rarely know the true odds.

climax.text: Ambiguity aversion explains why people avoid new investments, unfamiliar foods, and unknown paths—even promising ones.

punchline.text: We fear not knowing the odds more than bad odds.

quiz.question: What is ambiguity aversion?
options: Preferring known odds over unknown ones

details.summary: People prefer known risks over unknown risks, even when the unknown option has the same or better expected value. The Ellsberg paradox showed that participants choose a bag with known proportions over one with unknown proportions. Ambiguity aversion reflects discomfort with not knowing the odds.
details.whyItMatters: Ambiguity aversion explains why people avoid unfamiliar investments, technologies, and opportunities even when expected returns are favorable. It limits innovation and exploration.
takeaways: Known risks are preferred over unknown risks
The Ellsberg paradox demonstrates ambiguity aversion
Ambiguity aversion limits investment and innovation decisions

faq.question: What is the Ellsberg paradox?
faq.answer: An urn contains 30 red balls and 60 balls that are either black or yellow in unknown ratio. Most people prefer betting on red over black, revealing aversion to ambiguity. The paradox is that this preference violates expected utility theory, which treats both bets as equivalent.

faq.question: Is ambiguity aversion always irrational?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. When you do not know the odds, an adversary could exploit your ignorance. In competitive or adversarial environments, caution about unknown risks is sensible.
